analysis.one_liner: Phases out most "forever chemicals" from manufacturing and consumer products and bans their release into the environment.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS, or "forever chemicals," are a class of synthetic chemicals used in nonstick coatings, waterproof fabrics, food packaging, cosmetics, and industrial processes. They do not break down in the environment and have been found in the blood of most Americans and in drinking water supplies. This bill would phase out PFAS production for nonessential uses within ten years, ban PFAS in everyday products like carpets, food packaging, and cosmetics on faster timelines, and eventually make it illegal to release any detectable amount of PFAS into the environment. It would also let citizens sue violators, require companies to warn communities of PFAS emergencies, and preserve the right of people exposed to PFAS to sue for damages in state court. The bill never advanced past its initial referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, and especially the millions of Americans whose drinking water, food, and household products carry PFAS exposure: the bill would cut off new contamination at the source, require companies to warn and meet with communities hit by PFAS emergencies, and preserve state-court lawsuits for people harmed by exposure. Communities near manufacturing and release sites would gain the most, since the bill applies to federal agencies as well as private companies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to PFAS through water and products

how_it_helps.text: It would ban the sale of PFAS-containing carpets, fabric treatments, food packaging, juvenile products, and oil and gas products within one year, and cosmetics, furniture, apparel, and accessories within two years

It would require all manufacturers and users to fully phase out nonessential uses of PFAS within ten years, with each use presumed nonessential unless EPA designates it essential based on scientific review by the National Academies
After ten years it would make it unlawful to release any detectable amount of PFAS into the environment, with EPA inspections, monitoring, civil and criminal penalties, and citizen-suit enforcement

It would require companies causing PFAS emergencies to notify and hold public meetings in affected communities, preserve state-law damage suits for people harmed by exposure, and add a bankruptcy provision so PFAS defendants cannot escape cleanup and compensation obligations through court

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers and the industries that use the chemicals — textiles, cosmetics, food packaging, furniture, and oil and gas — would bear compliance, reformulation, and reporting costs, some of which would likely be passed to consumers as higher prices. Water and wastewater utilities are explicitly exempted from the bill's definitions, shifting the cost of treating already-contaminated water onto ratepayers and taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical makers and PFAS-using product manufacturers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would be broad: every manufacturer and user of PFAS — including importers of products known to contain them — must file phased-out plans and annual supplemental reports, and if EPA fails to finalize fees within two years the law sets a default supplemental report fee of $100,000, which small manufacturers may not be able to absorb
Product bans reach everyday goods — rugs, furniture, cosmetics, clothing, food packaging — and could raise prices or shrink product choices while safer substitutes are still being developed

Public water systems and wastewater treatment plants are explicitly excluded from the bill's definitions of manufacturer and user, so utilities that receive PFAS-contaminated waste bear no liability under the bill and the cost of cleaning already-contaminated water could fall on ratepayers and taxpayers

The full phaseout of nonessential uses takes 10 years after enactment, with the scientific review itself allowed to run three years, meaning exposure would continue for years even if the bill had passed

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit — less exposure to chemicals that persist in the body and the environment for generations — is large and durable, and the bill tried to cushion the transition with a decade-long phaseout, essential-use exceptions for uses with no safer alternative, and fee breaks for small manufacturers. The costs are real: compliance and reporting costs for a wide range of manufacturers (with a $100,000 default fee per report if EPA misses its deadline), likely pass-through to consumer prices, and a clean-up picture muddied by the exemption for water utilities, which could leave ratepayers and taxpayers covering treatment costs. On balance the trade favored ordinary people, and the bill's death means none of the benefits or costs were ever tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate environment committee for over eight months without a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on April 18, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the same day
No senator from either party joined as a cosponsor, leaving Durbin as the bill's only Senate supporter
The action history shows no markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor action after the referral for the remainder of the 118th Congress
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, and bills not passed by then die and must be reintroduced from scratch in a new Congress

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and the consumer product industries that use the chemicals are better off, because no phaseout, release ban, or litigation exposure was ever enacted. Communities with PFAS-contaminated water are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical makers and PFAS-using product industries

against.name: PFAS manufacturers and chemical industry groups
against.role: Chemical manufacturers and industry trade associations
against.what_they_did: Chemical makers facing multibillion-dollar PFAS cleanup and injury liabilities have broadly opposed comprehensive PFAS phaseout and liability legislation, arguing such bills would impose impossible compliance burdens and ban useful products.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough to reveal a partisan split: its only sponsor was a Democrat, and no senator of either party cosponsored it or acted on it.

industries.note: The bill phases out nonessential PFAS production within ten years, bans detectable releases, adds inspections and penalties, and includes a bankruptcy provision aimed at keeping PFAS makers on the hook for cleanup and injury claims. It would have converted a revenue stream that carries open-ended liability into a shrinking, closely policed one.

industries.industry: Consumer product makers using PFAS (textiles, cosmetics, food packaging, furniture)
industries.note: Fast product bans within one to two years would force these makers to reformulate rugs, clothing, cosmetics, furniture, and food packaging away from PFAS. Ordinary consumers bear some of the adjustment through prices, but are also the group the bans protect.

The bill explicitly excludes public water systems and treatment works from its definitions of manufacturer and user, so utilities that receive PFAS-contaminated waste avoid liability under the bill — but they would still have to treat contaminated water, with costs passed to ratepayers. The exclusion protects utilities while leaving cleanup costs with the public.
Oil and gas products containing PFAS face the fastest one-year sales ban in the bill, on top of the general release prohibition that applies across the economy.
